newsitem.title: IRAQ: Ekeus arrives in Baghdad for further arms talks.
newsitem.headline: Ekeus arrives in Baghdad for further arms talks.

text.p: Chief U.N. weapons inspector Rolf Ekeus arrived in Baghdad on Saturday for talks with Iraqi officials on outstanding disarmament issues, the Iraqi News Agency (INA) reported.
INA gave no further details. Ekeus was not available for comment as his Iraqi hosts took him to an undisclosed destination.

The visit by the Swedish head of the U.N. Special Commission (UNSCOM) dealing with Iraq is the latest in a series of missions by international arms experts to rid Baghdad of weapons of mass destruction under the 1991 Gulf War ceasefire.
Ekeus would be seeking proof of Iraq's claims to have done everything relevant to the disposal of proscribed items and materials.

He is expected to hold talks with Deputy Prime Minister Tareq Aziz and Oil Minister Amir Muhammad Rasheed, the former chairman of Iraq's Military Industrialisation Commission during his three-day visit.

Iraq gave Ekeus's deputy Charles Duelfer, who was in Baghdad this month, nine letters attempting to clarify its disclosure of banned weapons after the U.N. official said Iraq's original declarations were flawed and incomplete.
Ekeus told reporters in Bahrain his talks with Iraqi officials would help him assess his team's work over the last three months and set goals. Both sides agreed on the routine visit in June.
"Iraq admits that its has (arms) not accounted for...but they said these items were destroyed unilaterally and in that sense they were accounted for.
"Our programme is now to verify that the destruction indeed took place," Ekeus said on Friday.
Asked how many missiles Iraq might be hiding, Ekeus replied: "I said six to 16. We are trying to narrow the numbers now."
"We told the Security Council that we felt the dialogue on the political level has been fruitful...So we welcome that dialogue and we hope for tangible results," Ekeus said.

Iraq is seeking an all-clear from Ekeus, a key condition for allowing it free oil exports. But the envoy in a report this month said his commission could not yet account for small but significant amounts of prohibited items.
"It is a real matter of life and death for the states in the region, and therefore we cannot rest until we have accounted for them," he added.
Ekeus said in Bahrain 48 Iraqi missiles were handed over and destroyed under U.N. supervision after the Gulf War.
